full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury J: The Criminal Appeal No. 1205 of 2007 and the Jail Appeal Nos. 281 of 2007, 291 of 2007 and 303 of 2007, at the instance of the condemned-prisoners, are directed against the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 03-04-2007 passed by Mr SM Solaiman, Additional Sessions Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka in Sessions Case No. 90 of 2001 arising out of GR Case No. 668 of 2000 corresponding to Savar Police Station Case No. 34 dated 27-9-2000. By the impugned judgment and order, the learned Additional Sessions Judge convicted the accused-appellants under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code, 1860 and sentenced each of them thereunder to death. The learned Additional Sessions Judge also made a Reference to the High Court Division under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for confirmation of the death sentence imposed upon them. 

 5. At the commencement of the trial of the case, the learned trial Judge charged all the condemned-appellants under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code, 1860. The charge was read over and explained to them in the dock; but they pleaded not guilty thereto and claimed to be tried as per law. 

 12. Md Afzal Hossain also submits that although the confessional statements of the accused Shahid and Khorshed were brought to their notice at the time of their examination under section 342 of the Code, of Criminal Procedure; yet the fact remains that those confessional statements were not Spelt out in detail to them and; as such, they have been gravely prejudiced thereby and given this scenario, an Order may be passed for remanding the case to the trial' Court for freshman the stage of examination of the accused under section 342 Of the Code of Criminal Procedure: In Support of this Submission, Mr Md Afzal Hossain draws our attention to the decision in the case of Sohel @ Sanaullah @ Sohel Sanaullah vs State reported in 63 DLR (AD) 105. 

 13. Mr Md Afzal Hossain next submits that the alleged confessional statements of the accused Shahid and Khorshed were not recorded in their language; but in the language of the Magistrate and in that view of the matter, they admitted nothing and, as such, the learned trial Judge ought to have acquitted them of the charge levelled against them. On this point, Mr Md Afzal Hossain, adverts to the decision in the case of the State vs Abdur Rashid Piada alias Abdur Rashid Sardar reported in 40 DLR (AD) 106, 

 14. Mr Md Afzal Hossain also submits that the confessions of the accused have been made an, integral and substantial part of the prosecution version of the case, but the failure of the learned trial Judge to question them thereabout is clearly a serious omission which is not curable by the provisions of section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and this failure amounts to infringement of the provisions of section 342 of the said Code and that being so, the confessions will have to be excluded from consideration in determining their guilt. In support of this submission, Mr Md Afzal Hossain refers to the decision in the case of Rahim Baksh vs Crown reported in 4 DLR (FC) 53. 

 24. Mr Md Khurshedul Alam next submits that though there is no specific finding in the impugned judgment to the effect that the criminal act was done in furtherance of common intention of all the accused-appellants, yet this Court, being the last Court of facts, can arrive at such a finding on re-appraisal of the evidence and materials on record and in the facts and circumstances of the case inasmuch as, the powers and functions of the trial Court and those of the Appellate Court are co-extensive. In this regard, Mr Md Khurshedul Alam refers to the decision in the case of the State represented by the Solicitor, ministry of Law & Justice, Government of Bangladesh vs Montu alias Nazrul Haque & others reported in 44 DLR (AD) 287. 

 57. In the case of Nurul Haque vs State reported in 20 DLR 780, it was observed:— 

 "Now let us consider the value of a retracted confession as against the maker. On consideration of evidence on record, if it is found that a confession is voluntary and true, conviction of the maker himself can solely be based upon the same, no matter whether it is retracted or not. In the case of the State vs Minbun alias Gul Hassan reported in 16 DLR (Supreme Court) 598, their Lordships of the Supreme Court held as follows:.— 

 59. In the case of the State vs Punardhar Joydhar alias Kudu and Shefali reported in 31 DLR 312, it has been held that the accused first made a confessional statement under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that he committed that murder, although subsequently he retracted his confessional statement before the Court and the confession being found voluntary and without any threat, coercion or inducement, conviction of the accused based on his confession, though subsequently retracted by him, is valid in law. 

 60. The principle that has been enunciated in the case of Hazrat Ali vs State reported in 1990 BLD 38 = 42 DLR 177 is that once a confession has been found to be true and voluntary, conviction can be based solely on the confession, even if it is retracted. 

 61. The 'ratio decidendi' of the case of Bakul Chandra Sarkar vs State reported in 45 DLR 260 is that if a confession recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is true and voluntary, the same alone is sufficient for convicting the confessing accused and retraction of confession is immaterial, once it is found to be true and voluntary. 

 72. Incidentally, in the decision in the case of Babul alias Abdul Majid Khan vs State reported in 42 DLR (AD) 186, it was held, amongst others, in paragraph 10:— 

 73. Reverting to the case in hand, admittedly the police officer (PW 3) Sub-Inspector Md Mainul Islam who forwarded the condemned-appellants for recording of their confessions and the Magistrate himself (PW 4) Syed Lokman Ahmed have been examined to prove that they made the confessions which were recorded and produced before the Court Precisely speaking, by way of examination of the PW 3 Sub-Inspector. Md Mainul Islam and the PW 4 Syed Lokman Ahmed before the trial Court, the prosecution has definitely brought on record the minimum legal evidence to prove the commission of the offence by the condemned-prisoners. In our view, the requirement of bringing the minimum legal evidence in this case has been fulfilled as mandated by our Appellate Division in the decision reported in 42 DLR (AD) 186 (supra). 

 79. The other contention of Mr Md Afzal Hossain is that the confessional statements were not spelt out in detail to the accused at the time of their examination under section 342 of the code of Criminal Procedure, though they were referred to during the said examination, and such being the state of affairs, the case may be remanded to the trial from the stage of examination of the accused under section 342 of the said Code. But we are not impressed there-by. Admittedly, the confessional statements were brought to the notice of all condemned-appellants during their examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and during that examination, the inculpatory nature of the confessions was also pointed out to them; though those were not spelt out in detail. According to us, because of non-spelling out of the details of the confessions to the accused at the time of their examination under section 342 of the said Code, they have not been prejudiced in any way. So the case cannot be remanded to the trial Court for fresh trial as argued by Mr Hossain. In this regard, his reliance on the decisions in the cases of Sohel @ Sanaullah @ Sohel Sanaullah vs State; 63 DLR (AD) 105 and Rahim Baksh vs Crown; 4 DLR (FC) 53 is of no avail to him. 

 80. With regard to the contention of Mr Afzal Hossain that the confessions were not recorded in the language of the maker; but those were recorded in the language of the Magistrate and in this perspective, the accused admitted nothing in view of the decision in the case of the State vs Abdur Rashid Piada alias Abdur Rashid Sardar reported in 40 DLR (AD) 106, we are unable to accept the same for the simple reactor that no suggestion was put to the PW 4 Syed Lokman Ahmed to the effect that the confessions were not recorded in their language; rather those were recorded in the language of the Magistrate. Moreover, in that reported case, the Appellate Division has found that the alleged confessional statements are hardly confessional in nature, because neither of the accused admitted that he had taken part either in the assault upon the deceased Wazed or in the concealment of the dead body. But in the instant case, as we have found, all the condemned-appellants directly participated in the commission of the offence leading to the killing of Nasima as per their confessions.

 96. In the case of Bandez Ali vs State reported in 40 DLR (AD) 200, it was held at page 201:— 

 97. In the case of the State represented by the Solicitor to the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs Ashraf Ali reported in 46 DLR (AD) 241, it was observed by our Appellate Division in paragraph 5:— 

 98. In the present case before us, the manner of the occurrence as described. by all the condemned-appellants in their confessional statements and the injuries found on the persons of the deceased Nasima by Dr Sayeeda Chowdhury and Dr Mizanur Rahman during autopsies positively show that the criminal act was done with the intention of causing death of the victim Nasima thus attracting the ingredient of clause 'firstly' so section 300 of the Penal Code. Under the circumstances, we have no hesitation in holding that the criminal act committed by the accused Tipu, Shahid and Khorshed is culpable homicide amounting to murder punishable under section 302/34 of the Penal Code, 1860.
